# Introduction

The goal of today's lab is to briefly introduce you to the computing tools we'll use in
this course, set up your computing access, and complete the entry survey. We'll talk more
about these tools in lecture and in upcoming labs.

There is no statistics in today's lab, and nothing to hand in for a grade.

::: callout-note
## What is a container?

A container is a self-contained copy of RStudio for you, and you alone. All your computing
for this course happens inside it — no installation, no version mismatches between
sixteen different laptops.
:::

# Computing setup

## RStudio

::: callout-note
R is the name of the programming language itself and RStudio is a convenient interface.
:::

### Reserve your RStudio container

- Go to <https://cmgr.oit.duke.edu/containers>. Log in with your Duke NetID credentials.
- Click **"Reserve STA 119F"** to reserve an RStudio container. 

You only need to reserve a container once per semester.

### Open your RStudio container

- Go back to <https://cmgr.oit.duke.edu/containers> and log in again if needed.
- Click **`STA119F`** to open the container. You should now see the RStudio environment
  in your browser, with a **Console** pane showing a `>` prompt.

## Git and GitHub

In addition to R and RStudio, we'll use Git and GitHub for version control.

::: callout-note
Git is a version control system (like "Track Changes" in Microsoft Word, but far more
powerful) and GitHub is the home for your Git-based projects on the internet (like
Dropbox, but much better — and it makes collaboration visible).
:::

### Sign up for a GitHub account

You'll need a GitHub account to access the assignments and labs for this course.

- If you don't have one, go to [github.com](https://github.com/) and create one. Using
  your university email address is recommended but not required.
- If you already have an account, **log in right now and confirm you know your
  credentials** — don't assume. Too many failed login attempts locks the account **for
  the day**, which would end your participation in today's lab.

::: callout-tip
[Click here](https://happygitwithr.com/github-acct#username-advice) for advice on
choosing a username — it's a professional account you may still be using in ten years.
:::

## Connect RStudio and GitHub

Now that you have RStudio and a GitHub account, we'll configure Git so RStudio and GitHub
can talk to each other.

### Set up your SSH key

You'll authenticate to GitHub using SSH. **Follow along on the projector for this one** —
it's the step most likely to go sideways, and it's much easier to fix while everyone does
it together.

::: callout-note
You only do this once. Once the key exists, it keeps working — you won't repeat this in
any later lab.
:::

Type this in the **Console** and press Enter:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
credentials::ssh_setup_github()
```
:::


- **Step 1:** It asks *"No SSH key found. Generate one now?"* — press **1** for yes.
- **Step 2:** It generates a key (starting `ssh-rsa...`), then asks *"Would you like to
  open a browser now?"* — press **1**.
- **Step 3:** You may be asked for your GitHub username and password.
- **Step 4:** On the GitHub page that opens, **paste the key** into the box and give it a
  name — anything recognizable works, e.g. `histstat-container`.
- **Step 5:** Click the button to add the key.


### Configure Git to introduce yourself

Git labels every change with who made it, so it needs your name and email address.

Type this in the **Console**, with your own details substituted in:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name = "Your name",
  user.email = "Email associated with your GitHub account"
)
```
:::


For example:


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
usethis::use_git_config(
  user.name = "Jane Doe",
  user.email = "jane.doe@duke.edu"
)
```
:::


**Use the exact same email you used to create your GitHub account.** If these differ, Git
and GitHub won't connect your work to your account — the symptom is confusing rather than
obvious.

::: callout-tip
## How do I know I did it right?

Nothing visible happens, which is unnerving. To check: click the **Terminal** tab (next to
**Console**) and type:

```bash
git config user.name
git config user.email
```

Each should echo back exactly what you typed. If there's a typo, just run
`use_git_config()` again with the correction — the last one wins.
:::

# Clone your first repository

A **repository** ("repo") is a collection of files hosted on GitHub. Copying one down to
your container is called **cloning**.

::: callout-note
Today's repo is **public**, and there's nothing to commit or push yet — that starts in
**Lab 01**, which gets a full walkthrough of its own. Today is purely: does the pipeline work end to end, and can you read an error
message?
:::

1. Go to `https://github.com/.../lab-01`.
2. Click the green **Code** button. Choose **SSH** (it may already be selected — the
   label reads *Clone with SSH*), then click the clipboard icon to copy the address. It
   should start with `git@github.com:`, **not** `https://`.
3. In RStudio: **File → New Project → Version Control → Git**.
4. Paste the address into **Repository URL**. Leave the directory name as it fills in.
5. Click **Create Project**.

The first time your container talks to GitHub, you may see a message asking whether you
trust the host — *"the authenticity of host github.com can't be established."* Type
**yes** and press Enter.

::: callout-important
## If step 2 gave you an `https://` address

Go back and switch it to SSH. An `https://` address will ask for a password on every
single operation and will not accept your GitHub password — this is the single most
common way this step fails.
:::

RStudio will clone the repo and open it as a project. You should see its files in the
**Files** pane, bottom right.

**That's the whole skill.** You'll clone about one repo a week for the rest of the
semester, and after the third time you'll stop thinking about it.

# Tell me who you are

Fill in the entry survey: **[SURVEY-LINK]**

I use the answers for practical things — sending your GitHub organization invitation,
forming groups — and for one non-practical thing: I ask what you want out of the course
and what you're worried about. I read all sixteen. In week 8 I hand your own answers back
to you.

# Done

You now have a container, a GitHub account, a working SSH key, a configured Git, and a
cloned repository.

Next week: pull, commit, push, and the first real data — Mayer's 27 equations
(`labs/lab-01/`).

::: callout-tip
## If you got stuck

Come to office hours or send a message — **don't spend an evening fighting this alone,
and don't skip Lab 01 because today didn't finish.** Every later lab assumes today's setup
works, so a broken setup is the one problem worth interrupting me about.

If you finished early: **help the person next to you.** That's not extra credit, it's how
today goes well for everyone.
:::
